question:
The given sentence is divided into three segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error. If there is no error, select ‘No error’.
The volunteer gave on to / the food packets to the / children of the orphanage.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The volunteer gave on to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct phrasal verb to express distribution of something is "give out" (to distribute) or the simple verb "give...to" — not "give on to". The preposition "on" is redundant and grammatically wrong here.

• Rule — Redundant/Wrong Preposition: Certain verbs take a fixed preposition to form a phrasal verb with a specific meaning; adding an extra, unnecessary preposition (as in "gave on to") produces an ungrammatical construction.

• Corrected sentence: "The volunteer gave out the food packets to the children of the orphanage."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "the food packets to the" is grammatically correct as it stands — no error.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect because segment 1 does contain a grammatical error.

• Option 4: "children of the orphanage." is grammatically correct — no error.

NOTE

• Common confusions of this type tested by SSC: "give out" (distribute/announce), "give up" (quit), "give in" (surrender), "give away" (donate/reveal). Learn phrasal verbs as fixed units — inserting an extra preposition (like "on to" instead of "out") is a frequently tested error type.

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
It was my niece / who was leaving college / last year, and / not my son.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. who was leaving college.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "who was leaving college last year" wrongly uses the Past Continuous Tense ("was leaving") for an action that is a single, completed event tied to a definite point in the past ("last year").

• Rule — Past Continuous vs Simple Past: The Past Continuous Tense (was/were + V-ing) is used for an action that was in progress at a certain time in the past, or for a background action interrupted by another. A single, completed action that occurred at a definite past time must be expressed in the Simple Past Tense (V2).

• Corrected segment: "who left college" — Corrected sentence: "It was my niece who left college last year, and not my son."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "last year, and" is correct as it stands — it correctly specifies the definite past time and links the two parts of the sentence.

• Option 2: "not my son." is grammatically correct — no error.

• Option 3: "It was my niece" is a correct emphatic/cleft construction ("It was...who...") used to lay stress on the subject — no error.

NOTE

• The cleft sentence pattern "It was + noun + who/that + verb" is used to emphasise a particular part of the sentence.

• Frequently tested tense confusion: use Simple Past for a completed action at a specific past time (yesterday, last year, in 2020); use Past Continuous only for an ongoing action or a background action interrupted by another past action (e.g., "I was leaving when it started to rain").

question:
Parts of the given sentence have been underlined. One of them contains an error. The underlined parts are given as options with some changes. Select the option that correctly rectifies the error.
Raveena's daughter Kavya is most intelligent student and she consistently achieves top grades.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. an intelligent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original phrase "is most intelligent student" is incorrect because a singular countable noun (student) used after "is" must be preceded by an article, and "most" here is wrongly used as if it were a superlative degree marker without "the".

• Rule — Article with Singular Countable Noun: A singular countable noun used in a general, non-comparative sense must take the indefinite article "a/an". Since "intelligent" begins with a vowel sound, the article "an" is required: "an intelligent student".

• Rule — Superlative Degree: The superlative form "most intelligent" must always be preceded by "the" ("the most intelligent") and is used only when comparing three or more things. Here, no comparison is being made — the sentence simply describes Kavya — so the plain adjective "an intelligent" is correct, not the superlative.

• Corrected sentence: "Raveena's daughter Kavya is an intelligent student and she consistently achieves top grades."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Raveenas' daughter" is incorrect because it wrongly shifts the possessive apostrophe as if "Raveenas" were a plural noun; the original "Raveena's daughter" (singular possessive) is already correct.

• Option 2: "she has consistently" is incorrect because changing "she consistently achieves" to "she has consistently achieves" is grammatically wrong — the Present Perfect auxiliary "has" would require the past participle "achieved", not "achieves"; the original Simple Present form is correct.

• Option 4: "topper grades" is incorrect because "topper" is a noun (a person who tops a list), not an adjective, so it cannot modify "grades"; the original "top grades" is the correct usage.

NOTE

• Superlative degree always takes "the": the best, the tallest, the most beautiful.

• A singular countable noun in a general descriptive sense always needs an article: "a good boy", "an honest man", "an intelligent student".

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
UNICEF builds partnerships across the global community on accelerate gender equality.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. global community to accelerate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence needs an infinitive of purpose to explain why UNICEF builds partnerships — that is, in order to accelerate gender equality. The preposition "on" cannot be followed directly by the base form "accelerate".

• Rule — Infinitive of Purpose: To express the purpose/aim of an action, we use "to + base verb (V1)", e.g., "She works hard to succeed." Here, "to accelerate" correctly expresses the purpose of building the partnerships.

• Corrected sentence: "UNICEF builds partnerships across the global community to accelerate gender equality."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "global community with accelerate" is incorrect because the preposition "with" cannot be followed by the base verb "accelerate".

• Option 2: "global community till accelerate" is incorrect because "till" is a preposition of time and cannot be directly followed by a base verb either.

• Option 4: "global community in accelerate" is incorrect for the same reason — "in" cannot be followed by a bare base-form verb; it would need a gerund ("in accelerating"), which is not the option offered, and the intended meaning here is purpose, best expressed by the infinitive "to accelerate".

NOTE

• The infinitive of purpose ("to + V1") is a frequently tested SSC grammar point, e.g., "I woke up early to catch the train."

• Do not confuse it with the gerund form after a preposition (e.g., "committed to accelerating"), which requires "-ing", not the base verb.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option for each blank.
I was reading a book two days back. It was titled Charlie and the Chocolate Factory by Roland Dahl. It was fantastic. It has now become my favourite (1)________. It is about a boy named Charlie who is (2)________ poor. He wins a golden ticket that (3)________ him to enter the most famous chocolate factory in the world. He (4)________ it with his grandfather. But the other kids who accompany him are nasty. They are all spoilt. But you have to read the book to (5)________ out more about them. The amazing part of the book is that it is like a dream come true.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. book.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage is about the narrator reading a book — "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory" — and blank (1) must refer to this same word, describing what "has now become my favourite" item.

• Rule — Contextual/Collocation-based Cloze: In a cloze passage, each blank must be filled with the word that best fits both the grammatical structure and the overall meaning/context established earlier in the passage. Since the passage already establishes that a book was being read, "book" is the word that logically completes "has now become my favourite ___".

• Filled sentence: "It has now become my favourite book."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "text" is incorrect; while a book is a kind of text, "favourite text" is an unnatural and less precise collocation here compared to "favourite book", given the passage explicitly calls it a book.

• Option 2: "guide" is incorrect because a "guide" refers to an instructional or reference book, not a story book like the one described.

• Option 4: "manual" is incorrect because a "manual" is a technical instruction booklet, which does not fit a work of fiction like "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory".

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always re-read the surrounding sentences (not just the immediate blank) to identify the noun/word already established earlier in the passage.

• Common SSC cloze trap: choosing a near-synonym (like "text", "guide", "manual") instead of the word that matches the exact context already set by the passage.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option for each blank.
I was reading a book two days back. It was titled Charlie and the Chocolate Factory by Roland Dahl. It was fantastic. It has now become my favourite (1)________. It is about a boy named Charlie who is (2)________ poor. He wins a golden ticket that (3)________ him to enter the most famous chocolate factory in the world. He (4)________ it with his grandfather. But the other kids who accompany him are nasty. They are all spoilt. But you have to read the book to (5)________ out more about them. The amazing part of the book is that it is like a dream come true.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. very.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank modifies the adjective "poor" and must be filled with an intensifier that naturally combines with an adjective describing a state/condition. "Very poor" is the standard, natural collocation used to intensify the degree of poverty.

• Rule — Adverbs of Degree with Adjectives: Adverbs like "very" are used before an adjective to intensify its meaning (very poor, very tall, very happy). Adverbs of manner like "nicely" or "properly" describe how an action is done, not the degree of a state, and so cannot modify "poor" in this way.

• Filled sentence: "It is about a boy named Charlie who is very poor."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "nicely" is incorrect because it is an adverb of manner and cannot logically intensify the adjective "poor" ("nicely poor" is meaningless).

• Option 3: "properly" is incorrect for the same reason — it describes the manner of doing something, not the degree of a quality like poverty.

• Option 4: "finally" is incorrect because it is an adverb of time/sequence and does not fit the sense of intensifying "poor".

NOTE

• Common degree adverbs tested by SSC: very, quite, rather, extremely, too, so — each combines directly with an adjective to show intensity.

• Do not confuse adverbs of manner (nicely, properly, carefully) with adverbs of degree (very, quite, extremely) — only the latter can intensify an adjective like "poor".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option for each blank.
I was reading a book two days back. It was titled Charlie and the Chocolate Factory by Roland Dahl. It was fantastic. It has now become my favourite (1)________. It is about a boy named Charlie who is (2)________ poor. He wins a golden ticket that (3)________ him to enter the most famous chocolate factory in the world. He (4)________ it with his grandfather. But the other kids who accompany him are nasty. They are all spoilt. But you have to read the book to (5)________ out more about them. The amazing part of the book is that it is like a dream come true.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. allows.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes what the golden ticket does — it permits/enables Charlie to enter the chocolate factory. The verb that correctly expresses "giving permission or opportunity to do something" is "allows".

• Rule — Collocation with "to + verb": The verb "allow" is regularly followed by an object and an infinitive: "allow someone to do something" (e.g., "The ticket allows him to enter"). This is the standard structure used here: "that allows him to enter".

• Filled sentence: "He wins a golden ticket that allows him to enter the most famous chocolate factory in the world."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "bears" is incorrect because "bears him to enter" is not idiomatic English; "bear" does not collocate with "to enter" in this sense.

• Option 2: "gets" is incorrect because "gets him to enter" changes the sense to causing/persuading someone to do something reluctantly, which does not fit a golden ticket granting entry as a privilege.

• Option 3: "suffers" is incorrect because "suffer" means to undergo something unpleasant, which contradicts the positive context of winning a golden ticket.

NOTE

• Common SSC-tested causative/permissive verb pattern: allow/permit/enable + object + to + verb.

• Distinguish "allow" (give permission) from "make" (force, followed by bare infinitive) and "let" (permit, also followed by bare infinitive, without "to").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option for each blank.
I was reading a book two days back. It was titled Charlie and the Chocolate Factory by Roland Dahl. It was fantastic. It has now become my favourite (1)________. It is about a boy named Charlie who is (2)________ poor. He wins a golden ticket that (3)________ him to enter the most famous chocolate factory in the world. He (4)________ it with his grandfather. But the other kids who accompany him are nasty. They are all spoilt. But you have to read the book to (5)________ out more about them. The amazing part of the book is that it is like a dream come true.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. visits.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes what Charlie does at the chocolate factory along with his grandfather, after winning the golden ticket that allows him to enter it. The most contextually apt verb is "visits" — he pays a visit to / tours the factory with his grandfather.

• Rule — Context-based Verb Selection: In a cloze passage, the chosen verb must logically follow from the preceding sentence and fit the overall storyline. Since the previous sentence establishes that the ticket allows him to enter the factory, the natural next action is that he visits it (accompanied by his grandfather).

• Filled sentence: "He visits it with his grandfather."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "examines" is incorrect because "examines" suggests a close, technical inspection, which does not match the light, narrative tone of a boy touring a chocolate factory with his grandfather.

• Option 2: "explores" is incorrect because, although related in meaning, "explores" suggests independent discovery of unknown territory, which is a weaker fit than "visits" for describing accompanying someone to a place and being taken there as a guest.

• Option 4: "inspects" is incorrect because "inspects" implies a formal, official check for faults or compliance, which does not fit the context of a child enjoying a factory tour.

NOTE

• When multiple options seem close in meaning in a cloze passage, choose the one that best matches the narrative tone and the most natural real-world collocation, not merely a synonym that is technically related.

• "Visit" collocates naturally with places (visit a factory, visit a museum, visit a friend).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option for each blank.
I was reading a book two days back. It was titled Charlie and the Chocolate Factory by Roland Dahl. It was fantastic. It has now become my favourite (1)________. It is about a boy named Charlie who is (2)________ poor. He wins a golden ticket that (3)________ him to enter the most famous chocolate factory in the world. He (4)________ it with his grandfather. But the other kids who accompany him are nasty. They are all spoilt. But you have to read the book to (5)________ out more about them. The amazing part of the book is that it is like a dream come true.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. find.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank must complete the phrasal verb "find out", meaning to discover or learn something through effort — exactly the sense required here: reading the book to discover more information about the other children.

• Rule — Fixed Phrasal Verb: "Find out" is a fixed phrasal verb meaning "to obtain information about something / to discover a fact". The particle "out" is already printed after the blank in the passage ("to ___ out more about them"), so the blank must be filled with the verb "find" to complete this exact phrasal verb.

• Filled sentence: "But you have to read the book to find out more about them."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "unlearn" is incorrect because "unlearn out" is not a valid phrasal verb, and "unlearn" means to deliberately forget something previously learnt, which does not fit here.

• Option 3: "spot" is incorrect because "spot out" is not a standard English phrasal verb; "spot" means to notice or catch sight of something, which does not collocate with "out" in this way.

• Option 4: "locate" is incorrect because "locate out" is not a valid phrasal verb; "locate" means to find the exact position of something, which does not fit the idiomatic "find out more" construction.

NOTE

• "Find out" is one of the most frequently tested phrasal verbs in SSC exams, meaning to discover/learn information.

• Other common "find" phrasal verbs: find out about (discover), and related idioms like "get to the bottom of" (fully understand a problem).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Sluggish
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Rapid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Sluggish" means slow-moving, lacking energy or alertness; inactive. (सुस्त, मंद)
◦ Example: The traffic was sluggish during the heavy rain.

• The correct antonym is "Rapid", meaning happening or moving quickly; fast. (तीव्र, तेज़)
◦ Example: The company showed rapid growth in the last quarter.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hassled" (परेशान): Feeling harassed or bothered — not an antonym of "sluggish", as it relates to stress, not speed.

• Option 2: "Lethargic" (सुस्त): Means lacking energy, drowsy or sluggish — this is actually a synonym, not an antonym, of "sluggish".

• Option 3: "Leisurely" (इत्मीनान से): Means unhurried, relaxed in pace — this is close in meaning to "slow" and hence a near-synonym, not an antonym, of "sluggish".

NOTE

• Common synonym set for "sluggish": lethargic, languid, torpid, listless, inert.

• Common antonym set for "sluggish": rapid, brisk, swift, energetic, vigorous.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Timid
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Audacious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Timid" means showing a lack of courage or confidence; easily frightened; shy. (डरपोक, संकोची)
◦ Example: The timid child hid behind her mother when strangers approached.

• The correct antonym is "Audacious", meaning showing a willingness to take bold risks; fearlessly daring. (साहसी, निडर)
◦ Example: The audacious explorer set off alone into the uncharted jungle.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Resolute" (दृढ़निश्चयी): Means firm and determined in purpose — relates to firmness of decision, not directly to fearlessness, so it is a weaker antonym than "Audacious".

• Option 2: "Blunt" (रूखा): Means direct and straightforward in speech, sometimes to the point of rudeness — this relates to manner of speaking, not to courage, so it is not the antonym of "timid".

• Option 4: "Assertive" (दृढ़तापूर्वक अपनी बात कहने वाला): Means confident and direct in stating one's views — related to confidence in expression, but it is not as precise an opposite of "timid" (fearfulness) as "audacious" (boldness/daring) is.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "timid": shy, meek, diffident, timorous, apprehensive.

• Other antonyms of "timid" commonly seen in SSC vocabulary lists: bold, brave, daring, fearless, confident.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Retract
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Revoke.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Retract" means to withdraw a statement, promise, or accusation as being untrue or as no longer applying; to take back. (वापस लेना, प्रत्याहरण करना)
◦ Example: The witness retracted his earlier statement in court.

• The correct synonym is "Revoke", meaning to officially cancel or withdraw a decision, law, or agreement. (रद्द करना, वापस लेना)
◦ Example: The authorities revoked his driving licence after the accident.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Disturb" (परेशान करना): Means to interfere with or unsettle something — unrelated to withdrawing a statement.

• Option 2: "Please" (प्रसन्न करना): Means to give satisfaction or pleasure to someone — has no connection with taking something back.

• Option 3: "Implement" (क्रियान्वित करना): Means to put a decision or plan into effect — this is nearly opposite in sense to "retract" (withdrawing), not a synonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "retract": withdraw, recant, rescind, disavow, renounce.

• Commonly confused pair: "retract" (take back a statement) vs "retreat" (withdraw physically from a place) — SSC often tests this distinction.

question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.
Allusive handwriting creates a poor impression.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Illegible handwriting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Allusive" means "characterized by indirect references or allusions" and makes no sense when describing handwriting that "creates a poor impression". The intended word is "Illegible", meaning not clear enough to be read.

• Rule — Confusable Words: SSC frequently tests words that look or sound similar but have very different meanings. Here, "Allusive" (referring indirectly) is confused with "Illegible" (unreadable) — only the latter logically explains why handwriting would create a poor impression.

• Corrected sentence: "Illegible handwriting creates a poor impression."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Legal handwriting" is incorrect because "legal" (lawful) has no logical connection with handwriting creating a poor impression.

• Option 2: "Eligible handwriting" is incorrect because "eligible" means "qualified for something", which does not describe a quality of handwriting.

• Option 3: "Descriptive handwriting" is incorrect because "descriptive" (providing description) is not a quality that would make an impression poor.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word pairs tested by SSC: illegible/eligible, allusive/elusive/illusive, legible/legal.

• "Elusive" (difficult to find or catch) and "Illusive" (based on illusion, unreal) are also frequently confused with "Allusive" and "Illegible" — learn to distinguish all four.

question:
Select the option that rectifies the spelling of the underlined word in the given sentence.
It was a privvilege to receive the award from the President.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. privilege.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "privilege" — a special right, advantage, or immunity granted to a particular person or group.

• Spelling key: PRIVI + LEGE. Note there is only a single "v" and the word ends in "-lege", not "-ledge" or a doubled consonant.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "privilegge" is incorrect; it wrongly doubles the letter "g".

• Option 2: "privileege" is incorrect; it wrongly doubles the letter "e" before "ge".

• Option 4: "privillege" is incorrect; it wrongly doubles the letter "l".

NOTE

• Commonly misspelt words with silent/single letters often tested by SSC: privilege, occurrence, embarrass, harass, accommodate, questionnaire.

• Remember: "privilege" has no "d" (not "priviledge", a very common error) and no double "l" or double "g".

question: Select the sentence that brings out the most appropriate meaning of the idiom ‘Dog in the manger’.
option_1: Mohit was so loyal and committed to his company that he rejected lucrative offers from different companies.
option_2: To prove this is not a trap, I want to check the credibility of your plan.
option_3: Rachit had some important work and so he cancelled the show tickets for everyone.
option_4: You are here just because you have recognised your hidden potential.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Rachit had some important work and so he cancelled the show tickets for everyone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Dog in the manger" means a person who selfishly prevents others from having or enjoying something that they themselves do not need or cannot use. (टांग अड़ाने वाला व्यक्ति — जो स्वयं उपयोग न करे पर दूसरों को भी न करने दे)
◦ Example: He behaved like a dog in the manger when he refused to lend his old bicycle to anyone, even though he never rode it himself.

• In Option 3, Rachit, being unable to attend the show himself because of important work, cancelled the tickets for everyone else too — thereby denying others an enjoyment that he himself could not partake of. This is a textbook illustration of "dog in the manger" behaviour.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Describes loyalty and commitment (rejecting other job offers) — this illustrates devotion/faithfulness, not the "dog in the manger" idea of selfishly denying others.

• Option 2: Refers to checking credibility to avoid being tricked — this relates to caution/verification, not to selfishly withholding something.

• Option 4: Refers to recognising one's own hidden potential — this is about self-realisation, unrelated to denying others something one does not need.

NOTE

• The idiom originates from Aesop's fable in which a dog lay in a manger (feed trough) and snarled at the ox trying to eat the hay, even though the dog itself could not eat hay.

• Other idioms of selfishness commonly tested by SSC: "Cut off one's nose to spite one's face" (harm oneself out of spite), "Crab mentality" (pulling others down out of jealousy).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Alert
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Vigilant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Alert" means quick to notice danger or trouble; watchful and attentive. (सतर्क, चौकन्ना)
◦ Example: The alert guard noticed the suspicious package immediately.

• The correct synonym is "Vigilant", meaning keeping careful watch for possible danger or difficulties. (सतर्क, चौकस)
◦ Example: Citizens are urged to remain vigilant during the festival season.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Inactive" (निष्क्रिय): Means not active or functioning — this is nearly the opposite of "alert".

• Option 2: "Dull" (सुस्त): Means lacking sharpness or liveliness — again close to the opposite of "alert".

• Option 3: "Smart" (चतुर): Means clever or intelligent, but does not specifically convey watchfulness for danger, so it is a weaker match than "vigilant".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "alert": watchful, wary, attentive, observant.

• Antonyms of "alert" commonly tested: careless, negligent, inattentive, oblivious.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I find that students nowadays are not interested in ________ letters by hand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. writing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence discusses students not being interested in producing handwritten text, so the blank must be filled with the verb form that fits "___ letters by hand" — "writing".

• Rule — Gerund after Preposition: The preposition "in" must be followed by a gerund (verb + -ing), not a base verb. "Interested in writing" is the correct grammatical pattern.

• Filled sentence: "I find that students nowadays are not interested in writing letters by hand."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rioting" is incorrect because it means taking part in a violent public disturbance, which is unrelated to the context of letters and handwriting.

• Option 2: "rating" is incorrect because it means giving a rank or score to something, which does not fit "letters by hand".

• Option 4: "righting" is incorrect because it means correcting or setting something upright, and although it sounds identical to "writing", it is semantically wrong here.

NOTE

• "Writing" and "righting" are homophone-like sound traps frequently used in SSC exams — always check the meaning fits the context, not just the sound.

• The pattern "interested in + gerund" is a frequently tested preposition-gerund collocation (e.g., "interested in reading", "keen on learning").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
For Rana, unable to see a thing, the parade seemed to last forever.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. procession.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the given sentence, "parade" is used in its literal sense of a public march or procession of people, often for celebration or display. (जुलूस, परेड)
◦ Example: The Republic Day parade marched down the avenue for hours.

• The correct synonym is "procession", meaning a number of people or vehicles moving forward in an orderly, formal way. (जुलूस)
◦ Example: The wedding procession moved slowly through the crowded street.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hiding" (छिपना): Means concealing oneself from view — unrelated to the meaning of a public march.

• Option 2: "darkness" (अंधेरा): Means the absence of light — unrelated to "parade" in this context.

• Option 3: "concealment" (छिपाव): Means the act of hiding something — again unrelated to a procession or march.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "parade" (a public march/procession) with idiomatic uses like "parade one's wealth" (to show off).

• Related words: procession, cavalcade, march, cortege (a funeral procession).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Enormous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Minute.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Enormous" means very large in size, quantity, or extent; huge. (विशाल, बहुत बड़ा)
◦ Example: The company suffered enormous losses during the recession.

• The correct antonym is "Minute" (pronounced my-NEWT), meaning extremely small; tiny. (अत्यंत सूक्ष्म, बहुत छोटा)
◦ Example: Under the microscope, even a minute speck of dust looked huge.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Strong" (मज़बूत): Refers to physical or mental power, not size — unrelated to "enormous".

• Option 3: "Monstrous" (राक्षसी/विशालकाय): Means extremely large or ugly — this is actually a synonym, not an antonym, of "enormous".

• Option 4: "Tremendous" (जबरदस्त): Means very great in amount or scale — this too is a synonym, not an antonym, of "enormous".

NOTE

• Careful: "Minute" as an antonym here is an adjective (pronounced differently from the noun "minute" meaning 60 seconds) — a common SSC vocabulary trap.

• Other antonyms of "enormous": tiny, minuscule, microscopic, petite, diminutive.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to correct the sentence by using the denotation of the underlined word.
Mr. Sen is clever enough to handle his professional hazards.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Intelligent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The denotation (literal, dictionary meaning) of "clever" is mentally quick and resourceful; intelligent. (बुद्धिमान)
◦ Example: She is clever enough to solve the puzzle in minutes.

• Rule — Denotation vs Connotation: Denotation is the exact, literal dictionary meaning of a word, while connotation is the additional emotional or cultural association it carries (which can be positive or negative, e.g., "clever" can sometimes connote slyness). The question asks for the word based on the plain denotative meaning of "clever", which is "Intelligent".

• Reworded sentence: "Mr. Sen is intelligent enough to handle his professional hazards."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Foolish" (मूर्ख): Means lacking good sense — this is the opposite of "clever", not its denotation.

• Option 2: "Callous" (निर्दयी): Means insensitive or unfeeling — unrelated to the meaning of "clever".

• Option 4: "Bold" (साहसी): Means showing courage or confidence — this is a different quality from mental sharpness and is not the denotative meaning of "clever".

NOTE

• "Clever" can carry a negative connotation in some contexts (implying cunning or sly), but its core denotation remains "intelligent".

• Other word pairs where denotation/connotation differ: "cheap" (denotation: low cost; connotation: low quality), "childish" (denotation: like a child; connotation: immature, negative).

question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.
Although uncountable files stack up on the tables of government officials, they prefer doing their work at a more leisure pace.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. at a more leisurely pace.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "at a more leisure pace" wrongly uses the noun "leisure" as an adjective before the noun "pace". The correct adjective form is "leisurely".

• Rule — Adjective Formation: The noun "leisure" (free time) has the adjective form "leisurely" (unhurried, relaxed), formed by adding "-ly". Only the adjective form can directly modify a noun like "pace": "a leisurely pace".

• Corrected sentence: "Although uncountable files stack up on the tables of government officials, they prefer doing their work at a more leisurely pace."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "at a more leisure paced" is incorrect because it retains the noun "leisure" as a modifier and wrongly changes "pace" to "paced", which does not fit the structure "at a more ___ pace".

• Option 3: "No improvement needed" is incorrect because the original phrase "at a more leisure pace" does contain a grammatical error.

• Option 4: "at a more leisurely paced" is incorrect because, although it correctly changes "leisure" to "leisurely", it then wrongly changes the noun "pace" to "paced", producing an ungrammatical phrase ("a more leisurely paced" is not a complete noun phrase).

NOTE

• "Leisure" is a noun; "leisurely" is both an adjective and an adverb (e.g., "they walked leisurely").

• Similar noun-to-adjective "-ly" confusions tested by SSC: friend→friendly, cost→costly, love→lovely — note that "-ly" here forms an adjective, not an adverb, unlike most "-ly" adverbs.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
The technicians who were repairing the broken elevator called it a day.
option_3: Stopped to take a short break
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Stopped work for the day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to call it a day" means to decide to stop doing something, especially work, considering it finished for the time being. (काम को दिन भर के लिए बंद करना / काम समाप्त करना)
◦ Example: After working for ten hours straight, the workers decided to call it a day.

• In the given sentence, the technicians repairing the elevator decided to stop working and end their work for that day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Felt unhappy" is incorrect; the idiom has nothing to do with an emotional state of unhappiness.

• Option 2: "Shouted with anger" is incorrect; the idiom does not involve anger or shouting.

• Option 3: "Stopped to take a short break" is incorrect because "call it a day" means stopping work altogether for the day, not pausing briefly before resuming.

NOTE

• Related idiom: "to call it a night" — used similarly, but specifically for stopping an evening/night-time activity.

• Other work-related idioms tested by SSC: "burn the midnight oil" (work late into the night), "get down to business" (start working seriously).

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
The Chinese are believed to have a longer history than that of any other civilisation in the wolrd.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Wolrd.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Wolrd" is misspelt — the letters "l" and "r" have been transposed. The correct spelling is "World".

• Spelling key: W-O-R-L-D — remember the order "or" comes before "ld", not "ol" before "rd".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Civilisation" is correctly spelt (British spelling, with "s"; the American variant uses "z" — "Civilization" — both are acceptable, and the printed British form here is correctly spelt).

• Option 3: "Believed" is correctly spelt — follows the rule "i before e except after c" (believe).

• Option 4: "Chinese" is correctly spelt — no error.

NOTE

• Letter transposition (swapping the order of two adjacent letters) is one of the most common SSC spelling-error patterns — always read each word letter by letter rather than skimming.

• Other frequently transposed-letter traps: "freind"/"friend", "recieve"/"receive", "thier"/"their".

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the bracketed word segment in the following sentence.
Classical buildings in ancient Greek and Roman times were (characteristically built) from marble or some other attractive, durable stone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. typically built.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed phrase "characteristically built" is not the most natural or precise way to express that classical buildings were usually/commonly constructed from marble or similar stone. The correct substitute is "typically built", meaning usually or normally built.

• Rule — Precision of Word Choice: SSC often tests replacement of a word/phrase with one that conveys the intended meaning more accurately and idiomatically. "Typically" (usually, as a general rule) fits the sense of describing a common building practice far better than "characteristically" (in a way distinctive/particular to something).

• Corrected sentence: "Classical buildings in ancient Greek and Roman times were typically built from marble or some other attractive, durable stone."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "fascinating to build" is incorrect because it changes the meaning to describe the process of building as fascinating, not the frequency/manner of the material used.

• Option 3: "strange build" is grammatically and semantically incorrect — it neither fits the sentence structure nor conveys the intended meaning of common building practice.

• Option 4: "mainly having been built" is incorrect because it is an awkward, unidiomatic construction that disrupts the simple past passive structure of the sentence ("were ... built").

NOTE

• Distinguish "characteristically" (in a manner distinctive to a particular person/thing) from "typically" (usually, as a general rule) — a frequently tested confusable adverb pair.

• Keep the passive voice structure "were + built" intact when selecting a replacement — the chosen option must grammatically slot into this frame.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The housing loan taken by Ramesh effected his daily expenses adversely.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. by Ramesh affected.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "effected" is used incorrectly here. The intended meaning is that the loan influenced/impacted Ramesh's daily expenses, which requires the verb "affected", not "effected".

• Rule — Affect vs Effect: "Affect" is a verb meaning to influence or have an impact on something. "Effect" is usually a noun meaning a result or consequence (and, less commonly, a verb meaning "to bring about/cause"). Since the sentence needs a verb meaning "influenced", "affected" is correct, not "effected".

• Corrected sentence: "The housing loan taken by Ramesh affected his daily expenses adversely."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "for Ramesh effected" is incorrect because it retains the wrong verb "effected" and also wrongly changes the preposition "by" to "for" — the loan was taken by Ramesh, not for him in this context.

• Option 3: "from Ramesh effected" is incorrect for the same reasons — it keeps "effected" and wrongly changes "by" to "from".

• Option 4: "of Ramesh effected" is incorrect because it retains "effected" and wrongly changes "by" to "of", which does not fit the passive construction "the loan taken by Ramesh".

NOTE

• Classic SSC confusable pair: "affect" (verb: to influence) vs "effect" (noun: a result; rarely a verb meaning "to bring about", e.g., "to effect change").

• Memory aid: Affect = Action (verb); Effect = End result (noun).
